l: kings of the earth, Psalms, Chapter 138
s: The kings of the earth are said to be those who will give thanks to the LORD because they have heard the words of his mouth. They will also sing of the ways of the LORD, for his glory is great.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 139
s: Chapter 139 is a psalm attributed to David, addressed to the LORD, for the Chief Musician. David declares that the LORD has searched and known him completely, including his movements, thoughts, words, and ways. He says there is nowhere he could flee from the LORD's Spirit and presence, whether heaven, Sheol, the uttermost parts of the sea, or darkness. He praises the LORD for forming him in the womb and for writing his ordained days in a book. He then asks God to kill the wicked, whom he hates as enemies, and closes by asking God to search him, know his heart, and lead him in the everlasting way.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 139
s: The LORD is addressed as the one who has searched and known David, perceiving his thoughts, words, paths, and ways. He is present everywhere, formed David in the womb, wrote David's days in his book, and has thoughts toward David too vast to count. David asks him to search his heart, test him, and lead him in the everlasting way.

l: David, Psalms, Chapter 139
s: David, the psalm's author, marvels that the LORD knows him fully and cannot be escaped, and thanks him for being fearfully and wonderfully made. He expresses hatred for those who hate God, calling them his enemies, and asks God to kill the wicked. He ends by inviting God to search his heart and thoughts, see if any wicked way is in him, and lead him in the everlasting way.

l: the wicked (enemies of God), Psalms, Chapter 139
s: The wicked are described as bloodthirsty men who speak against God wickedly and take his name in vain. David asks God to kill them and tells them to get away from him. He says he hates them with perfect hatred and counts them as his enemies.

l: God's omniscience and omnipresence, Psalms, Chapter 139
s: The psalm portrays God as knowing everything about David: his sitting and rising, his thoughts from afar, his path, his ways, and every word before it is spoken. God is also present in heaven, Sheol, the farthest sea, and the darkness, which is like light to him. His knowledge is described as too lofty for David to attain.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 140
s: Chapter 140 is a psalm attributed to David, addressed to the Chief Musician, in which the speaker begs the LORD for deliverance from evil and violent men. These enemies plot mischief, gather for war, sharpen their tongues like serpents, and hide snares and traps for his feet. The speaker affirms that the LORD is his God and the strength of his salvation, who covered his head in the day of battle. He asks that the wicked not succeed and that burning coals, fire, and miry pits fall on those who surround him. The psalm closes with confidence that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted and the needy, and that the righteous will give thanks and dwell in his presence.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 140
s: The LORD is asked to deliver and preserve the speaker from evil and violent men, and to keep him from the hands of the wicked. He is called God and the strength of the speaker's salvation, who covered his head in the day of battle. The speaker is confident that he will maintain the cause of the afflicted and justice for the needy, and that the upright will dwell in his presence.

l: David, Psalms, Chapter 140
s: David, named as the author of this psalm for the Chief Musician, cries out to the LORD for rescue from violent men who plot against him with snares, traps, and venomous words. He declares the LORD to be his God and recalls being covered in the day of battle. He expresses confidence that the LORD will uphold the afflicted and the needy.

l: evil men (David's enemies), Psalms, Chapter 140
s: The evil men devise mischief in their hearts, gather continually for war, and sharpen their tongues like a serpent with viper's poison under their lips. The proud among them hide snares, nets, and traps by the path to trip the speaker's feet. The speaker asks that their plans fail and that their own lips' mischief cover them, with burning coals, fire, and miry pits falling on them, and states that an evil speaker won't be established on the earth and evil will hunt the violent man to overthrow him.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 141
s: In this psalm of David, the psalmist calls on the LORD to come quickly and hear his prayer, asking that it be received like incense and the evening sacrifice. He asks the LORD to guard his mouth and keep his heart from evil, from joining the deeds of those who work iniquity, and from eating their delicacies. He welcomes correction from the righteous as kindness and oil on the head, while his prayer stays set against evil deeds. The judges of the wicked are thrown down by the rock, and their bones are scattered at the mouth of Sheol. The psalmist takes refuge in the LORD and asks to be kept from the snares of the workers of iniquity, praying that the wicked fall into their own nets while he passes by.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 141
s: The LORD is called on by the psalmist to come quickly, listen, set a watch before the psalmist's mouth, and keep his heart from evil. He is addressed as the one in whom the psalmist takes refuge and whom the psalmist's eyes are on. The psalmist asks him not to leave his soul destitute and to keep him from the snares of the wicked.

l: speaker (the psalmist), Psalms, Chapter 141
s: The psalmist, identified as David in the heading, calls urgently on the LORD and asks to be guarded in speech and heart. He refuses to share in the deeds or delicacies of those who work iniquity and welcomes reproof from the righteous. He takes refuge in the LORD and asks to be kept from snares while the wicked fall into their own nets.

l: workers of iniquity, Psalms, Chapter 141
s: The workers of iniquity practice deeds of wickedness, and the psalmist asks not to eat of their delicacies. They have laid a snare and traps for him. The psalmist prays that the wicked fall together into their own nets while he passes by.

l: righteous one, Psalms, Chapter 141
s: The righteous one is described as striking and reproving the psalmist, which the psalmist says would be kindness and like oil on the head. The psalmist asks that his head not refuse it.

l: prayer (the psalmist's prayer), Psalms, Chapter 141
s: The psalmist asks that his prayer be set before the LORD like incense, with the lifting up of his hands like the evening sacrifice. He also says his prayer is always against evil deeds.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 142
s: Chapter 142 is a prayer of David, described as a contemplation from when he was in the cave. David cries aloud to the LORD, pouring out his complaint and troubles, and says that although his spirit is overwhelmed the LORD knows his route, along which a snare has been hidden for him. He laments that no one at his right side is concerned for him and that no refuge or care remains, yet he declares the LORD to be his refuge and portion in the land of the living. He asks the LORD to hear his cry and deliver him from persecutors who are too strong for him, and to bring his soul out of prison so he may give thanks and the righteous may surround him.

l: David, Psalms, Chapter 142
s: David, in the cave, cries aloud to the LORD and pours out his complaint and troubles. He says his spirit is overwhelmed, that a snare has been hidden on his path, and that no one cares for his soul, yet he calls the LORD his refuge and portion. He asks to be delivered and brought out of prison so he can give thanks to the LORD's name.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 142
s: The LORD is the one David cries to for mercy, and David says the LORD knew his route when his spirit was overwhelmed. David calls him his refuge and his portion in the land of the living, and asks him to hear, deliver, and free him, expecting that the LORD will be good to him.

l: persecutors (David's persecutors), Psalms, Chapter 142
s: David's persecutors are described as too strong for him. They have hidden a snare for him on the path he walks, and he asks the LORD to deliver him from them.

l: prayer (David's prayer), Psalms, Chapter 142
s: David's prayer is spoken aloud with his voice and takes the form of a complaint and a plea for mercy. It moves from describing his troubles and abandonment to declaring the LORD his refuge, then asks for a hearing, deliverance from persecutors, and release from prison so he may give thanks. It ends with the expectation that the righteous will surround him because the LORD will be good to him.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 143
s: Chapter 143 is a psalm of David in which he pleads with the LORD to hear his prayer and relieve him, while acknowledging that no living person is righteous before God. David says his enemy has pursued him, struck his life to the ground, and made him dwell in dark places like the long dead, leaving his spirit overwhelmed and his heart desolate. He recalls the days of old, meditates on the LORD's works, spreads out his hands, and thirsts for God like parched land. He asks to hear the LORD's loving kindness in the morning, to be taught the way to walk and to do God's will, and to be led by God's good Spirit. He closes by asking the LORD to revive him, bring him out of trouble, cut off his enemies, and destroy those who afflict his soul, because he is God's servant.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 143
s: The LORD is addressed by David as the one who hears prayer and acts in faithfulness and righteousness. David asks him to answer quickly, not hide his face, deliver him from enemies, teach him his will, lead him with his good Spirit, revive him, and cut off his enemies. David calls him his God and appeals to his loving kindness and his name's sake.

l: David, Psalms, Chapter 143
s: David, the psalm's author, pleads for relief, confessing that no living person is righteous in God's sight. He describes being pursued and struck down by an enemy, with his spirit overwhelmed and heart desolate, yet he remembers God's past works, thirsts for him, and trusts him. He asks for guidance, deliverance, revival, and the destruction of his afflicters, identifying himself as God's servant.

l: enemy (David's enemy), Psalms, Chapter 143
s: The enemy pursues David's soul and has struck his life down to the ground. He has made David live in dark places like those long dead. David asks the LORD to deliver him from his enemies, cut them off, and destroy all who afflict his soul.

l: prayer (David's prayer), Psalms, Chapter 143
s: David's prayer opens with a plea that the LORD hear his petitions and relieve him, and it continues through requests for a quick answer, deliverance, guidance, and revival. It includes spreading out his hands and a soul thirsting like parched land. It ends with a request that the LORD cut off his enemies, based on David being God's servant.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 144
s: Chapter 144, attributed to David, opens by blessing the LORD as his rock, fortress, deliverer and shield who trains him for battle and subdues his people under him. David reflects on the frailty of man, whose days are like a passing shadow, and asks the LORD to part the heavens, send lightning and arrows, and rescue him from great waters and from foreigners whose mouths speak deceit and whose right hands are false. He promises to sing a new song to God on a ten-stringed lyre, praising him as the one who gives salvation to kings and rescues his servant David from the deadly sword. The chapter closes by repeating the plea for rescue and picturing a blessed people with thriving sons and daughters, full barns, multiplying sheep, strong oxen and secure, quiet streets, declaring happy the people whose God is the LORD.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 144
s: The LORD is blessed as David's rock, loving kindness, fortress, high tower, deliverer, shield and refuge, who trains his hands for war and subdues his people under him. David asks him to part the heavens, touch the mountains, throw lightning and send arrows, and to rescue him from the foreigners. He is described as the one who gives salvation to kings, and the people whose God he is are called happy.

l: David, Psalms, Chapter 144
s: David, named as the author, praises the LORD as his protector and trainer for battle, and reflects on how fleeting man is. He pleads to be rescued from great waters and from foreigners, and vows to sing a new song with a ten-stringed lyre. He is identified as the LORD's servant, rescued from the deadly sword.

l: foreigners, Psalms, Chapter 144
s: The foreigners are described as people whose mouths speak deceit and whose right hand is a right hand of falsehood. David twice asks the LORD to rescue and deliver him out of their hands.

l: prosperity of the people, Psalms, Chapter 144
s: The chapter pictures a prosperous people whose sons are like well-nurtured plants and whose daughters are like carved pillars adorning a palace. Their barns are full of every kind of provision, their sheep produce thousands and ten thousands, their oxen pull heavy loads, and there is no breaking in, no going away and no outcry in the streets. Such people are called happy, especially because their God is the LORD.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 145
s: Chapter 145 is a praise psalm by David in which he vows to exalt God, the King, and praise his name every day forever. David declares the LORD's greatness unsearchable and says each generation will commend his works and mighty acts to the next. The psalm describes the LORD as gracious, merciful, slow to anger, good to all, and faithful, with an everlasting kingdom and dominion through all generations. It says the LORD upholds those who fall, feeds every living thing, is near to all who call on him in truth, and preserves those who love him while destroying the wicked. David closes by promising to speak the LORD's praise and calling on all flesh to bless his holy name forever.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 145
s: The LORD is addressed as God and King and is called great, unsearchable in greatness, gracious, merciful, slow to anger, good to all, righteous, and faithful. He upholds those who fall, raises the bowed down, feeds every living thing, and is near to all who call on him in truth. He fulfills the desire of those who fear him, hears and saves them, preserves those who love him, and will destroy all the wicked.

l: saints, Psalms, Chapter 145
s: The saints of the LORD are said to extol him along with all his works. They will speak of the glory of his kingdom and talk about his power, making known to the sons of men his mighty acts.

l: throne and kingdom of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 145
s: The kingdom of the LORD is described as glorious and majestic, and as an everlasting kingdom. His dominion is said to endure throughout all generations, and the saints will speak of its glory.

l: works of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 145
s: The LORD's works are called wondrous, mighty, and awesome, and one generation will commend them to another. His tender mercies are over all his works, he is gracious in all his works, and all his works will give thanks to him.

l: praise, Psalms, Chapter 145
s: David vows to praise the LORD's name every day and forever, to extol him, meditate on his majesty, and declare his greatness. He says the LORD is greatly to be praised, that generations and the saints will join in it, and he closes by calling all flesh to bless the LORD's holy name forever and ever.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 146
s: Chapter 146 is a song of praise in which the speaker calls on his own soul to praise the LORD and vows to sing to God for as long as he lives. He warns against trusting princes, who are mortal: their spirits depart, they return to the earth, and their thoughts perish that same day. He declares happy the one whose help and hope is the God of Jacob, the maker of heaven, earth, and sea, who keeps truth forever. The LORD is described as executing justice for the oppressed, feeding the hungry, freeing prisoners, opening the eyes of the blind, raising the bowed down, loving the righteous, preserving foreigners, upholding the fatherless and widow, and overturning the way of the wicked. The chapter ends by affirming that the LORD will reign forever, as Zion's God to all generations.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 146
s: The LORD is praised as the God of Jacob, who made heaven, earth, the sea, and all in them, and who keeps truth forever. He executes justice for the oppressed, gives food to the hungry, frees prisoners, opens the eyes of the blind, raises those bowed down, loves the righteous, preserves foreigners, upholds the fatherless and widow, and turns the way of the wicked upside down. He will reign forever as Zion's God to all generations.

l: speaker (psalmist), Psalms, Chapter 146
s: The speaker urges his own soul to praise the LORD and vows to praise and sing to God as long as he lives and exists. He warns against trusting princes and pronounces happy the person whose help and hope are in the LORD, the God of Jacob. He closes by calling for praise of the LORD.

l: princes, Psalms, Chapter 146
s: Princes are named as those in whom trust should not be placed, since a son of man offers no help. The text says his spirit departs, he returns to the earth, and on that very day his thoughts perish.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 147
s: Chapter 147 is a psalm calling people to praise the LORD, who builds up Jerusalem, gathers Israel's outcasts, heals the brokenhearted, and numbers and names the stars. It contrasts his care for the humble and those who fear him with his bringing down of the wicked, and says he takes no pleasure in the strength of horses or the legs of a man. The LORD is shown covering the sky with clouds, sending rain, making grass grow, and feeding livestock and young ravens. Jerusalem and Zion are urged to praise him for strengthened gates, blessed children, peace in the borders, and the finest wheat. His word runs swiftly to the earth, sending snow, frost, and hail and then melting them, and he has shown his word, statutes, and ordinances to Jacob and Israel but not to other nations.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 147
s: The LORD builds up Jerusalem, gathers Israel's outcasts, heals the brokenhearted, and counts and names the stars. He is great, mighty, and infinite in understanding, upholds the humble, brings the wicked down, and provides for livestock and young ravens. He takes pleasure in those who fear him and hope in his loving kindness, not in the strength of horses or the legs of a man.

l: Jerusalem, Psalms, Chapter 147
s: Jerusalem is built up by the LORD and is called, along with Zion, to praise its God. He has strengthened the bars of its gates, blessed its children, made peace in its borders, and filled it with the finest wheat.

l: Israel, Psalms, Chapter 147
s: The LORD gathers together the outcasts of Israel. He shows his word, statutes, and ordinances to Jacob and Israel, and has not done this for any other nation, which do not know his ordinances.

l: those who fear him (the LORD's favored), Psalms, Chapter 147
s: The LORD takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his loving kindness. Their favored status is set against his lack of delight in the strength of the horse or the legs of a man.

l: weather (the LORD's control of clouds, rain, snow, frost, hail, wind), Psalms, Chapter 147
s: The LORD covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for the earth, and makes grass grow on the mountains. He gives snow like wool, scatters frost like ashes, and hurls down hail like pebbles, so that no one can stand before his cold. He then melts them by sending out his word and causing his wind to blow so that the waters flow.

l: word of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 147
s: The LORD's commandment goes out to the earth and his word runs very swiftly. His word melts the snow, frost, and hail. He shows his word, with his statutes and ordinances, to Jacob and Israel.

l: praise, Psalms, Chapter 147
s: The psalm opens and closes with the call to praise the LORD, saying it is good, pleasant, and fitting. It urges singing with thanksgiving and praises on the harp, and directs Jerusalem and Zion to praise their God.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 148
s: Chapter 148 is a call for all creation to praise the LORD. It first summons the heavens, including angels, his army, sun, moon, stars, and the waters above the heavens, to praise him because he commanded and they were created and established forever. It then summons the earth, including sea creatures, weather, mountains, trees, animals, kings, peoples, judges, and people of every age, to praise his name, which alone is exalted. The chapter ends by noting that he has lifted up the horn of his people, the children of Israel, a people near to him.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 148
s: The LORD is the one whom the heavens and the earth are called to praise. He commanded and the heavenly beings and bodies were created, established them forever, and made a decree that will not pass away. His name alone is exalted, his glory is above earth and heavens, and he has lifted up the horn of his people.

l: heavens, Psalms, Chapter 148
s: The heavens are called to praise the LORD, along with angels, his army, sun, moon, shining stars, and the waters above them. They were created at his command and established forever and ever under a decree that will not pass away. His glory is said to be above them.

l: earth, Psalms, Chapter 148
s: The earth is called to praise the LORD through sea creatures, depths, lightning, hail, snow, clouds, stormy wind, mountains, hills, trees, wild and domestic animals, birds, kings, peoples, princes, judges, and people of all ages. The stormy wind is described as fulfilling his word. His glory is said to be above the earth.

l: Israel, Psalms, Chapter 148
s: Israel, called the children of Israel, is identified as the LORD's people, whose horn he has lifted up. They are described as his saints and as a people near to him, and their praise is mentioned in the closing verse.

l: praise of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 148
s: Praise of the LORD is the chapter's central command, repeated to the heavens and then to the earth, and it is to be given to his name. The reason given is that he created all things by his command and that his name alone is exalted. The chapter opens and closes with 'Praise the LORD!'

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 149
s: Chapter 149 calls on the assembly of the saints to praise the LORD with a new song. Israel and the children of Zion are urged to rejoice in their Maker and King, praising his name with dance, tambourine, and harp. The LORD is said to take pleasure in his people and to crown the humble with salvation. The saints are told to rejoice in honor and sing for joy on their beds, with high praises of God in their mouths and a two-edged sword in their hands. The sword is for executing vengeance and punishments on the nations and peoples, binding their kings and nobles with chains and iron fetters, and carrying out the written judgment, which is an honor for all his saints.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 149
s: The LORD is praised with a new song and is named as the maker of Israel and the King of the children of Zion. He takes pleasure in his people and crowns the humble with salvation. The judgment to be executed on the nations is described as written and as his.

l: Israel, Psalms, Chapter 149
s: Israel is called to rejoice in him who made them. Together with the children of Zion, they are urged to be joyful in their King and to praise his name with dance, tambourine, and harp.

l: saints, Psalms, Chapter 149
s: The saints form the assembly in which the new song is sung, and they are told to rejoice in honor and sing for joy on their beds. They are to have high praises of God in their mouths and a two-edged sword in their hands to execute vengeance, punishments, and the written judgment. The text says all his saints have this honor.

l: nations, Psalms, Chapter 149
s: The nations, along with the peoples, are the targets of vengeance and punishments to be executed by the saints. Their kings are to be bound with chains and their nobles with fetters of iron, as the written judgment is carried out on them.

l: praise of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 149
s: Praise is the central call of the chapter, opening and closing it with "Praise the LORD!" It is to be expressed in a new song, in the dance, with tambourine and harp, and in high praises of God in the mouths of the saints.

l: vengeance and punishments, Psalms, Chapter 149
s: Vengeance and punishments are to be executed on the nations and peoples by the saints, who hold a two-edged sword. They include binding kings with chains and nobles with iron fetters, carrying out the written judgment, which is called an honor for all his saints.

l: Psalms, Psalms, Chapter 150
s: Chapter 150 is a closing call to praise the LORD. It tells the reader to praise God in his sanctuary and in his heavens, for his acts of power, his mighty acts, and his excellent greatness. It lists the means of praise: trumpet, harp and lyre, tambourine and dancing, stringed instruments and flute, and loud, resounding cymbals. It ends by calling on everything that has breath to praise the LORD.

l: LORD, Psalms, Chapter 150
s: The LORD is the one to be praised in his sanctuary and in his heavens. He is praised for his acts of power, his mighty acts, and his excellent greatness. The chapter opens and closes with the command to praise him.

l: everything that has breath, Psalms, Chapter 150
s: Everything that has breath is called on in the final verse to praise the LORD. This universal summons ends the chapter.

l: praise, Psalms, Chapter 150
s: Praise is commanded repeatedly throughout the chapter, directed at the LORD in his sanctuary and heavens and for his acts of power, mighty acts, and greatness. It is to be expressed with trumpet, harp, lyre, tambourine, dancing, stringed instruments, flute, and loud, resounding cymbals. The chapter closes by extending it to everything that has breath.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John / Chapter 1
s: John chapter 1 opens by declaring that the Word was with God and was God, made all things, and became flesh as Jesus Christ, full of grace and truth. John, a man sent from God, testifies about the light, denies being the Christ, Elijah, or the prophet when priests and Levites from the Pharisees question him, and calls himself the voice crying in the wilderness. He identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God and the Son of God after seeing the Spirit descend on him like a dove. Two of John's disciples, one of them Andrew, follow Jesus, and Andrew brings his brother Simon, whom Jesus renames Cephas (Peter). Jesus then calls Philip, who finds Nathanael, and Nathanael confesses Jesus as Son of God and King of Israel after Jesus tells him he saw him under the fig tree.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John / Chapter 1
s: Jesus is presented as the Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh full of grace and truth. John identifies him as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit, and the Son of God. He invites two disciples to come and see where he stays, renames Simon as Cephas, calls Philip to follow him, tells Nathanael he saw him under the fig tree, and promises that they will see heaven opened and angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man.

l: God, The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John / Chapter 1
s: God is described as the one with whom the Word was in the beginning, and no one has seen God at any time, though the only born Son has declared him. God sent John to baptize in water and told him that the one on whom he saw the Spirit descend and remain is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. Those who receive and believe in the Word are given the right to become God's children, born of God.

l: John, The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John / Chapter 1
s: John is a man sent from God as a witness to testify about the light, though he himself was not the light. He denies being the Christ, Elijah, or the prophet, calls himself the voice crying in the wilderness, and baptizes in water at Bethany beyond the Jordan. He testifies that Jesus is the Lamb of God and the Son of God after seeing the Spirit descend on him, and two of his disciples follow Jesus as a result.

l: Andrew, The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John / Chapter 1
s: Andrew is one of the two disciples of John who heard him call Jesus the Lamb of God and followed Jesus, staying with him that day. He is identified as Simon Peter's brother and from Bethsaida. He first finds his brother Simon, tells him they have found the Messiah, and brings him to Jesus.

l: Simon Peter, The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John / Chapter 1
s: Simon, brother of Andrew, is told by Andrew that the Messiah has been found and is brought to Jesus. Jesus looks at him, calls him Simon the son of Jonah, and says he will be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter. He is also named as being from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Philip.

l: Philip, The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John / Chapter 1
s: Philip is from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter, and is found by Jesus, who says to him, "Follow me." He then finds Nathanael and tells him they have found the one of whom Moses and the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. When Nathanael doubts, Philip answers, "Come and see."

l: Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John / Chapter 1
s: Nathanael is found by Philip, who tells him about Jesus of Nazareth, and he doubts that anything good can come out of Nazareth. Jesus calls him an Israelite indeed in whom is no deceit and says he saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael then declares Jesus the Son of God and King of Israel, and Jesus promises he will see greater things.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: At a wedding in Cana of Galilee on the third day, Jesus' mother tells Jesus the wine has run out, and after the servants fill six stone water pots at his word, the water becomes wine that the ruler of the feast praises. John calls this the beginning of Jesus' signs, and his disciples believe in him. Jesus then goes down to Capernaum with his mother, brothers, and disciples, and later goes up to Jerusalem for the Passover. There he drives the sellers of oxen, sheep, and doves and the money changers out of the temple with a whip of cords, and the Jews ask for a sign. Jesus answers that if they destroy this temple he will raise it in three days, which the text explains refers to his body, and the disciples remember this after he is raised from the dead; many believe in his name, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: Jesus is invited with his disciples to the wedding in Cana, where he tells the servants to fill the water pots and the water becomes wine, revealing his glory. He later goes to Capernaum and then Jerusalem, drives the sellers and money changers from the temple, and speaks of destroying and raising up the temple of his body. He does not entrust himself to those who believe in him at the Passover, because he knows everyone and what is in man.

l: Mary (Jesus' mother), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: Jesus' mother is at the wedding in Cana and tells Jesus, "They have no wine." After his reply that his hour has not yet come, she tells the servants to do whatever he says. She later goes down to Capernaum with Jesus, his brothers, and his disciples.

l: disciples (Jesus' disciples), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: The disciples are invited with Jesus to the wedding and believe in him after he reveals his glory there. They go with him to Capernaum, and at the temple they remember the Scripture "Zeal for your house will eat me up." After he is raised from the dead, they remember his words about the temple and believe the Scripture and his word.

l: wedding (in Cana of Galilee), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: The wedding takes place on the third day in Cana of Galilee, with Jesus, his mother, and his disciples present. When the wine runs out, Jesus provides wine, and the ruler of the feast calls the bridegroom and praises him for keeping the good wine until now.

l: wine, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: The wine runs out at the wedding, prompting Jesus' mother to speak to him. Water drawn from the filled pots becomes wine, and the ruler of the feast, not knowing its source, calls it the good wine kept until now, better than what is usually served first.

l: water pots (at the wedding), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: Six stone water pots stand at the wedding for the Jews' way of purifying, each holding two or three metretes. At Jesus' command the servants fill them to the brim with water, and what is drawn from them is wine.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: At the temple the Jews ask Jesus what sign he shows for doing these things. When he says he will raise up the destroyed temple in three days, they object that it took forty-six years to build it and misunderstand that he speaks of his body.

l: temple (in Jerusalem), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: The temple in Jerusalem is where Jesus finds people selling oxen, sheep, and doves and changing money at the Passover, and he drives them out, calling it his Father's house. Jesus says that if this temple is destroyed he will raise it in three days, and the text says he spoke of the temple of his body. The Jews note it took forty-six years to build.

l: sellers and money changers (in the temple), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: Those selling oxen, sheep, and doves and the money changers sitting in the temple are driven out by Jesus with a whip of cords. He pours out the changers' money, overturns their tables, and tells the dove sellers to take their things away and not make his Father's house a marketplace.

l: temple cleansing, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: Before the Passover, Jesus makes a whip of cords and drives out the sheep, oxen, and sellers, pours out the money, and overturns the tables. His disciples recall the words "Zeal for your house will eat me up," and the Jews respond by asking him for a sign.

l: signs of Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 2
s: The turning of water into wine at Cana is called the beginning of his signs, and it reveals his glory and leads his disciples to believe. At the Passover in Jerusalem many believe in his name as they observe the signs he does, and the Jews ask what sign he shows for cleansing the temple.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler of the Jews, comes to Jesus by night and acknowledges him as a teacher from God. Jesus tells him that one must be born anew, of water and Spirit, to see and enter God's Kingdom, and Nicodemus is puzzled. Jesus explains that God so loved the world that he gave his only born Son so that whoever believes should not perish but have eternal life, and that people are judged by whether they come to the light or love the darkness. Jesus then goes into Judea and baptizes while John baptizes at Enon near Salim, and John's disciples report that everyone is going to Jesus. John replies that he is not the Christ, that he is the bridegroom's friend, and that Jesus must increase while he must decrease, adding that the Father loves the Son and that those who believe the Son have eternal life.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: Jesus is visited by Nicodemus at night and teaches him that one must be born anew, of water and Spirit, to enter God's Kingdom. He speaks of himself as the Son of Man who descended from heaven and will be lifted up, and as the Son God gave so the world might be saved. He then goes into Judea with his disciples, stays there and baptizes, and John's disciples report that everyone is coming to him.

l: Nicodemus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: Nicodemus is introduced as a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews who comes to Jesus by night, calling him a teacher from God because of his signs. He misunderstands the idea of being born anew, asking whether a man can enter his mother's womb a second time, and asks 'How can these things be?' Jesus rebukes him as the teacher of Israel who doesn't understand these things.

l: God, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: God is said to have so loved the world that he gave his only born Son, not to judge the world but so that it would be saved through him. God gives the Spirit without measure to the one he sent, and the person who accepts the Son's witness sets a seal that God is true. The wrath of God remains on those who disobey the Son.

l: John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: John is baptizing in Enon near Salim, where there is much water, and has not yet been thrown into prison. When his disciples complain that Jesus is baptizing and everyone is going to him, John answers that a man can receive only what is given from heaven. He says he is not the Christ but was sent before him, likens himself to the bridegroom's friend who rejoices, and declares 'He must increase, but I must decrease.'

l: new birth, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: Jesus tells Nicodemus that unless one is born anew, or born of water and Spirit, he can't see or enter God's Kingdom. He distinguishes what is born of the flesh, which is flesh, from what is born of the Spirit, which is spirit, and compares the Spirit's work to the wind, whose source and destination are unknown. Nicodemus takes it literally and does not understand.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: God's Kingdom is something one can't see unless born anew and can't enter unless born of water and Spirit. It is mentioned in Jesus's first two statements to Nicodemus.

l: eternal life, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: Eternal life is promised to whoever believes in the Son, who will not perish. It is linked to the Son being lifted up as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness. John adds that one who believes in the Son has eternal life, while one who disobeys won't see life.

l: judgment, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: Jesus says God did not send his Son to judge the world but to save it. The one who believes is not judged, while the one who doesn't believe has been judged already for not believing in the name of the only born Son. The judgment is that the light has come into the world and men loved the darkness because their works were evil.

l: light and darkness, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 3
s: Light is said to have come into the world, but men loved darkness rather than light because their works were evil. Everyone who does evil hates the light and avoids it so his works are not exposed. The one who does the truth comes to the light so that his works may be revealed as done in God.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: Jesus leaves Judea after the Pharisees hear he is making more disciples than John, and passes through Samaria, where he rests at Jacob's well near Sychar. There he speaks with a Samaritan woman, offering her living water, telling her about her five husbands, teaching that true worshipers worship the Father in spirit and truth, and revealing that he is the Messiah. The woman tells her city, many Samaritans believe, and after Jesus stays two days they declare him the Savior of the world. Jesus then goes to Galilee, where a nobleman from Capernaum begs him to heal his dying son. Jesus says the son lives, the man believes and goes home, and his servants confirm the child recovered at the very hour Jesus spoke, in what is called the second sign Jesus did after coming out of Judea.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee via Samaria, where, tired, he sits at Jacob's well and speaks with a Samaritan woman, offering her living water, exposing her marital history, and declaring that he is the Messiah. He stays two days with the Samaritans, who call him the Savior of the world, then goes to Galilee, where he heals a nobleman's son at a distance with the words "Your son lives." The text notes that he himself did not baptize, and that this was his second sign after coming out of Judea.

l: Samaritan woman, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: A woman of Samaria comes to draw water at Jacob's well and is asked by Jesus for a drink, which surprises her because Jews have no dealings with Samaritans. After he speaks of living water and tells her about her five husbands, she perceives he is a prophet, raises the question of where to worship, and hears him say he is the Messiah. She leaves her water pot, tells the people of the city to come see a man who told her everything she had done, and her testimony leads many to believe.

l: disciples (Jesus' disciples), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: Jesus' disciples baptize on his behalf and have gone into the city to buy food while he talks with the woman. On returning they marvel that he is speaking with a woman, urge him to eat, and misunderstand when he says he has food they don't know about. Jesus tells them his food is to do the will of the one who sent him, and that he sent them to reap what others have labored for.

l: Samaritans, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: Many Samaritans from the city believe in Jesus because of the woman's testimony, come out to him, and beg him to stay, and he remains two days. Many more believe because of his own word, and they tell the woman they now know for themselves that he is the Christ, the Savior of the world.

l: Galilee, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: Jesus departs into Galilee after leaving Judea and again after his two days in Samaria. The Galileans receive him because they saw what he did at the feast in Jerusalem, though Jesus testifies that a prophet has no honor in his own country. In Cana of Galilee, where he earlier made water into wine, he heals the nobleman's son.

l: Jacob's well, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: Jacob's well is at Sychar in Samaria, near the parcel of ground Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Jesus sits by it, tired from his journey, around the sixth hour, and the conversation with the Samaritan woman takes place there. The woman notes it is deep and that Jacob gave it, and that he, his children, and his livestock drank from it.

l: living water, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that if she knew the gift of God and who was asking her for a drink, she would have asked him and he would have given her living water. He explains that those who drink ordinary water will thirst again, but the water he gives will become in a person a well springing up to eternal life. The woman asks for this water so she will not thirst or have to come to draw.

l: worship, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: The woman raises the dispute between worshiping on the Samaritan mountain and in Jerusalem. Jesus replies that the hour is coming, and now is, when neither place will matter and true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, since the Father seeks such worshipers and God is spirit. He also says the Samaritans worship what they do not know, while "we" worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.

l: nobleman, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: A nobleman whose son is sick at Capernaum goes to Jesus at Cana and begs him to come down and heal the boy, who is at the point of death. Jesus remarks that people will not believe without signs and wonders, but then says "Go your way. Your son lives." The man believes Jesus' word and goes, and when his servants meet him with news of recovery, he and his whole house believe.

l: nobleman's son, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: The nobleman's son lies sick at Capernaum, at the point of death with a fever. His father's servants report that he lives, and he is learned to have begun to get better the day before at the seventh hour, the very hour Jesus said "Your son lives."

l: healing of nobleman's son, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 4
s: Jesus heals the nobleman's son from a distance by saying "Your son lives," without going to Capernaum. The fever left the boy at the seventh hour the previous day, matching the time Jesus spoke, which leads the father and his whole house to believe. The text calls it the second sign Jesus did after coming out of Judea into Galilee.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 5
s: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for a feast and at the Bethesda pool heals a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years, telling him to take up his mat and walk. Because it is the Sabbath, the Jews object to the man carrying his mat, and after the man learns who healed him and tells them it was Jesus, they persecute and seek to kill Jesus. Jesus answers that his Father is still working and so is he, and he describes the Son's dependence on the Father, his power to give life and to judge, and the coming resurrection of life or of judgment. He then lists the witnesses to himself: John, his works, the Father, and the Scriptures. He concludes that the Jews will not come to him for life and that Moses, in whom they hope, will accuse them.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 5
s: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem, heals the man at Bethesda on the Sabbath, and later finds him in the temple and tells him to sin no more. He claims that his Father is still working and so is he, that the Son does only what he sees the Father doing, gives life, and has been given all judgment. He cites John, his works, the Father and the Scriptures as testimony about himself, and says Moses wrote about him.

l: God, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 5
s: God is called Jesus' Father, and Jesus says he is still working, loves the Son, shows him all he does, and raises the dead and gives them life. He has given all judgment to the Son and has life in himself, which he gave the Son also to have. He has himself testified about Jesus, though the Jews have never heard his voice or seen his form.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 5
s: The Jews tell the healed man it is not lawful to carry his mat on the Sabbath and ask who told him to do so. Once told it was Jesus, they persecute him and seek all the more to kill him, because he broke the Sabbath and called God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Jesus tells them they search the Scriptures but will not come to him for life, lack God's love, and receive glory from one another, and that Moses, on whom they set their hope, accuses them.

l: man healed at Bethesda (sick for thirty-eight years), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 5
s: The man had been sick for thirty-eight years and tells Jesus he has no one to put him into the pool when the water is stirred. At Jesus' command he is made well immediately, takes up his mat and walks. He does not know who healed him, tells the Jews it was the one who made him well, and after Jesus finds him in the temple and warns him, he tells the Jews it was Jesus.

l: Bethesda, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 5
s: Bethesda is a pool in Jerusalem by the sheep gate, called this in Hebrew, with five porches. A great multitude of sick, blind, lame and paralyzed people lay there waiting for the water to move, since the first one in after an angel stirred it was healed. It is the place where Jesus heals the man who had been sick for thirty-eight years.

l: Sabbath, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 5
s: The day Jesus heals the man at Bethesda is a Sabbath. The Jews say it is not lawful for the man to carry his mat on that day, and they persecute Jesus and seek to kill him because he did these things on the Sabbath. They are further angered because he broke the Sabbath and also called God his own Father.

l: testimony about Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 5
s: Jesus says that if he testified only about himself his witness would not be valid, and that another testifies about him. He names John, who testified to the truth, his own works which the Father gave him, the Father himself, and the Scriptures. He says the Jews do not believe these witnesses and will not come to him for life.

l: resurrection and judgment, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 5
s: Jesus says the Father has given all judgment to the Son, who also gives life to whom he desires, and that those who hear his word and believe the one who sent him have eternal life and have passed out of death into life. He says the hour comes when all in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who did good to the resurrection of life and those who did evil to the resurrection of judgment. He says the Son has authority to execute judgment because he is a son of man, and that his own judgment is righteous.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: Jesus crosses the sea of Galilee, where a great multitude follows him, and he feeds about five thousand men with a boy's five barley loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over. The multitude wants to make him king, so he withdraws to the mountain, and his disciples cross the sea at night until he comes to them walking on the water. The next day the multitude finds him at Capernaum, and he tells them to seek the food that remains to eternal life, declaring himself the bread of life who came down from heaven and whose flesh and blood give life. The Jews murmur and contend, many disciples turn back saying it is a hard saying, and Simon Peter, answering for the twelve, confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus then says that one of the twelve is a devil, referring to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, who would betray him.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: Jesus feeds the multitude, withdraws when they try to make him king, and walks on the sea to his disciples. At Capernaum he teaches that he is the bread of life who came down from heaven, and that his flesh and blood give eternal life. He knows who does not believe and who will betray him, and he says one of the twelve is a devil.

l: Simon Peter, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: Simon Peter, Andrew's brother, answers for the twelve when Jesus asks if they also want to leave. He says they have nowhere else to go because Jesus has the words of eternal life, and confesses him as the Christ, the Son of the living God.

l: disciples (Jesus' disciples), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: The disciples distribute the loaves and fish, gather twelve baskets of pieces, and row across the sea in the dark, where they see Jesus walking on the water. Later many of them find his teaching a hard saying and go back, while the twelve remain, one of them being Judas who would betray Jesus.

l: multitude (following Jesus), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: The great multitude follows Jesus because of his signs on the sick, is fed by him, and calls him the prophet who comes into the world. They intend to take him by force to make him king, then cross by boat to Capernaum seeking him. Jesus tells them they seek him for the loaves, not for the signs, and they ask for the bread he speaks of.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: The Jews murmur when Jesus says he is the bread that came down out of heaven, pointing out that they know his father and mother as the son of Joseph. They then contend with one another over how he can give his flesh to eat.

l: God the Father, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: The Father sent Jesus and has sealed him, gives the true bread out of heaven, and gives people to Jesus. No one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws him or it is given by him. Jesus says he came to do the Father's will, that he lose nothing of all given to him and raise them at the last day.

l: sea of Tiberias, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: Jesus goes to the other side of the sea of Galilee, also called the Sea of Tiberias. A great wind tosses the sea as the disciples row across it, and they see Jesus walking on it.

l: feeding of the five thousand, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: At Passover time Jesus asks Philip where to buy bread, to test him, and has the people sit on the grass. About five thousand men are fed, and the multitude then calls him the prophet who comes into the world. Jesus afterward says the multitude seeks him because they ate and were filled.

l: loaves and fish, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: A boy's five barley loaves and two fish, which Andrew says are little among so many, are taken by Jesus, who gives thanks and distributes them. All eat as much as they desire, and twelve baskets of broken pieces are left from the loaves.

l: Jesus walking on the sea, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: At night, after rowing about twenty-five or thirty stadia, the disciples see Jesus walking on the sea and drawing near the boat, and they are afraid. He tells them "It is I. Don't be afraid," and immediately the boat is at the land where they were going.

l: manna, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: The multitude cites the manna their fathers ate in the wilderness as a sign, quoting that God gave them bread out of heaven. Jesus replies that Moses did not give it, that the Father gives the true bread, and that the fathers ate manna and died.

l: bread of life discourse (true bread from heaven), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: In the synagogue at Capernaum Jesus says he is the bread of life and the living bread that came down from heaven, and that whoever comes to and believes in him will not hunger or thirst. The teaching about eating his flesh divides his hearers, leading to murmuring, contention, and many disciples departing.

l: eternal life, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: Jesus says the food that remains leads to eternal life and that the Son of Man will give it. He says everyone who sees the Son and believes has eternal life and will be raised at the last day, and that eating this bread means living forever. Peter says Jesus has the words of eternal life.

l: Jesus's flesh and blood, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: Jesus says the bread he will give for the life of the world is his flesh, and that unless people eat his flesh and drink his blood they have no life in themselves. He calls his flesh food indeed and his blood drink indeed, and says those who eat and drink live in him and he in them. The Jews ask how he can give his flesh, and many disciples find it a hard saying.

l: belief in Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 6
s: Jesus says the work of God is to believe in the one he sent, and that whoever believes in him will never be thirsty and has eternal life. Some of those who saw him do not believe, and he says no one can come unless the Father gives it. Many disciples leave, but Peter confesses belief that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: During the Feast of Booths, Jesus stays in Galilee to avoid the Jews who seek to kill him, rejects his unbelieving brothers' urging to go to Judea publicly, then goes up secretly and teaches in the temple midway through the feast. He says his teaching comes from the one who sent him, defends his Sabbath healing, and tells the crowd he will be with them only a little while longer. The multitude is divided over whether he is a good man, the prophet, or the Christ, with some objecting that he comes from Galilee. The Pharisees and chief priests send officers to arrest him, but the officers return without him, saying no man ever spoke like him. Nicodemus asks that the law be followed in hearing Jesus, and the others rebuke him before everyone goes home.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: Jesus avoids Judea because the Jews seek to kill him, declines his brothers' call to reveal himself, and goes up to the feast in secret. He teaches in the temple that his teaching is from the one who sent him, defends healing on the Sabbath, and on the last day of the feast invites the thirsty to come and drink, promising rivers of living water for those who believe. He says he will be with them a little while longer and that they will seek him and not find him.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: The Jews seek to kill Jesus and look for him at the feast, asking where he is. They marvel at his learning and puzzle over his saying that they cannot come where he is, wondering if he will go to the Dispersion among the Greeks. People fear them, so no one speaks openly about Jesus.

l: brothers (Jesus' brothers), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: Jesus' brothers urge him to leave Galilee and go into Judea to show his works openly to the world. The text states that they did not believe in him. They go up to the feast ahead of him.

l: the multitude, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: The multitude murmurs about Jesus, with some calling him a good man and others saying he leads people astray. One answer to him is that he has a demon, and many believe in him because of his signs. They are divided, some calling him the prophet, some the Christ, and others objecting that the Christ does not come from Galilee.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: The Pharisees hear the multitude murmuring about Jesus and, with the chief priests, send officers to arrest him. When the officers return without him, they ask whether the officers were also led astray and say that no rulers or Pharisees believe in him. They call the multitude, who do not know the law, cursed.

l: the chief priests, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: The chief priests join the Pharisees in sending officers to arrest Jesus. They question the officers when they come back without him.

l: officers (sent by the chief priests and Pharisees), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: The officers are sent to arrest Jesus but return without him. They explain to the chief priests and Pharisees, "No man ever spoke like this man!"

l: Nicodemus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: Nicodemus, identified as the one who came to Jesus by night and as one of the Pharisees' group, asks whether the law judges a man without first hearing from him and knowing what he does. The others answer by asking if he is also from Galilee and tell him to search and see that no prophet has arisen from there.

l: God the Father, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: God is referred to as the one who sent Jesus, and Jesus says his teaching is not his own but this sender's. Jesus says the sender is true, that the crowd does not know him, and that Jesus knows him because he is from him. Jesus says that he will go to the one who sent him.

l: Feast of Booths, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: The Feast of Booths is at hand and sets the occasion for the chapter. Jesus' brothers go up to it, Jesus follows secretly, and he teaches in the temple in the middle of it. On its last and greatest day he cries out his invitation to the thirsty.

l: Galilee, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 7
s: Jesus walks in Galilee and stays there to avoid Judea, where the Jews seek to kill him. Some in the multitude doubt he is the Christ because he comes from Galilee, and the others tell Nicodemus that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: In John 8, Jesus teaches in the temple, where the scribes and the Pharisees bring a woman taken in adultery and test him about stoning her; he challenges the sinless to throw the first stone, and after her accusers leave he tells her he does not condemn her and to sin no more. He then declares himself the light of the world, and the Pharisees dispute his testimony, which he says is validated by the Father who sent him. In a long dispute with the Jews, including those who had believed him, Jesus speaks of truth and freedom, sin as bondage, and their descent from Abraham versus the devil. The Jews accuse him of having a demon, and when he says Abraham rejoiced to see his day and 'before Abraham came into existence, I AM,' they take up stones, but he hides himself and leaves the temple.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: Jesus teaches in the temple, writes on the ground, and challenges the accusers of the woman, then tells her he does not condemn her and to sin no more. He declares himself the light of the world, says he is from above and sent by the Father, and claims that Abraham saw his day and that before Abraham existed, 'I AM.' The Jews take up stones against him, but he hides himself and goes out of the temple.

l: God the Father, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: Jesus says the Father sent him, is with him, and testifies about him alongside his own testimony. Jesus says he speaks what he heard from and was taught by the Father, always does what pleases him, and that the Father glorifies him. The Jews claim God as their one Father, but Jesus says they do not know him.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: With the scribes, the Pharisees bring the woman taken in adultery to Jesus and cite Moses' law on stoning to test him and find something to accuse him of. Later they tell Jesus his self-testimony is not valid after he calls himself the light of the world. They ask where his Father is and are told they know neither him nor the Father.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: The Jews question Jesus' words about going away, and many of them believe in him after he speaks. Jesus tells those who had believed that remaining in his word makes them disciples, but they object that they are Abraham's offspring and never in bondage, and he says they seek to kill him. They accuse him of being a Samaritan with a demon, doubt that he has seen Abraham, and take up stones to throw at him.

l: woman taken in adultery, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: The woman is brought by the scribes and Pharisees, who say she was caught in the very act, and is set in the middle. After her accusers leave one by one, she tells Jesus that no one condemned her. Jesus says he does not condemn her either and tells her to go her way and sin no more.

l: Abraham, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: The Jews claim Abraham as their father and say they are his offspring. Jesus replies that Abraham's children would do Abraham's works and that Abraham did not seek to kill as they do. He says Abraham rejoiced to see his day, saw it and was glad, and declares that before Abraham came into existence, he is. The Jews note that Abraham died, as did the prophets.

l: the devil, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: Jesus tells the Jews that they are of their father the devil and want to do his desires. He describes the devil as a murderer from the beginning who does not stand in the truth, has no truth in him, speaks lies on his own, and is a liar and the father of lies.

l: stoning of the woman, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: The scribes and Pharisees cite Moses' command to stone such women and ask Jesus what he says. Jesus says the one without sin should throw the first stone, and the accusers leave one by one, oldest first, so the stoning does not happen. Later, the Jews take up stones to throw at Jesus himself, but he escapes.

l: sin, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: Jesus says the one without sin may throw the first stone, and tells the woman to sin no more. He says that those who do not believe he is he will die in their sins, and that everyone who commits sin is a bondservant of sin. He asks which of his accusers convicts him of sin.

l: truth and freedom, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 8
s: Jesus tells those who believed him that if they remain in his word they will know the truth and the truth will make them free. They protest that they have never been in bondage, and he answers that everyone who commits sin is sin's bondservant, a bondservant does not remain in the house forever, and if the Son makes them free they will be free indeed. He says he tells the truth, which they do not believe, while the devil has no truth in him.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: Jesus sees a man blind from birth and, after telling his disciples that the blindness is not due to sin but so that the works of God might be revealed, he anoints the man's eyes with mud made from spit and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam. The man returns seeing, and his neighbors argue over whether he is the same person. Because the healing happened on a Sabbath, the Pharisees interrogate him, divide among themselves, and call his parents, who confirm he was born blind but defer to him out of fear of being put out of the synagogue. The healed man defends Jesus as a prophet and as someone from God, and the Pharisees insult him and throw him out. Jesus finds him, the man believes and worships him, and Jesus tells the Pharisees that their claim to see leaves their sin in place.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: Jesus tells his disciples the man's blindness is neither his own nor his parents' sin but a way for God's works to be revealed, and declares himself the light of the world. He makes mud with spit, anoints the man's eyes, and sends him to wash at Siloam, then later finds him after he is expelled and reveals himself as the Son of God, accepting his worship. He says he came for judgment so that those who don't see may see and those who see may become blind, and tells the Pharisees their sin remains.

l: blind man (healed by Jesus), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: The man, blind from birth, is healed after washing at Siloam as Jesus directed, and he identifies himself to doubting neighbors as the one who begged. Under repeated questioning by the Pharisees he calls Jesus a prophet, says he does not know whether Jesus is a sinner but knows he now sees, and argues that Jesus must be from God. He is thrown out, then believes in Jesus as Lord and worships him.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: The Pharisees question the healed man about how he received sight, and they split over whether Jesus can be from God given that he did the healing on the Sabbath. They call his parents, insult the man, claim to be disciples of Moses while saying they don't know where Jesus comes from, and throw the man out. When Jesus says those who see may become blind, some of them ask if they are also blind, and he says their sin remains.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: The Jews do not believe the man had been blind and received sight until they summon his parents. They had already agreed that anyone who confessed Jesus as Christ would be put out of the synagogue, which makes the parents afraid. They call the man a second time, tell him to give glory to God, and assert that Jesus is a sinner.

l: parents (the blind man's parents), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: The parents are asked whether the man is their son and whether he was born blind, and they confirm both. They say they don't know how he now sees or who opened his eyes, and tell the questioners to ask him since he is of age. The text says they answer this way because they fear the Jews and expulsion from the synagogue.

l: pool of Siloam, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: Jesus sends the blind man to wash in the pool of Siloam, a name explained as meaning "Sent." The man goes, washes, and returns seeing, and he later cites the pool in telling others how he received his sight.

l: God, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: Jesus says the man's blindness exists so that the works of God might be revealed, and refers to God as the one who sent him. The Pharisees claim God spoke to Moses, and the healed man argues that God does not listen to sinners but listens to a worshiper who does his will, so Jesus must be from God. The Pharisees tell the man to give glory to God.

l: mud (Jesus' mud), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: Jesus spits on the ground, makes mud with the saliva, and anoints the blind man's eyes with it. The man later describes this to neighbors and Pharisees as how Jesus opened his eyes, and the making of mud is noted as having occurred on a Sabbath.

l: healing of the blind man, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: A man blind from birth receives sight after Jesus anoints his eyes with mud and he washes at Siloam, an event the text says happened on a Sabbath. It causes disputes among the neighbors and divides the Pharisees, who debate whether a sinner could do such signs. The man notes that it has never been heard of since the world began that anyone opened the eyes of someone born blind.

l: blindness and sight (spiritual), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 9
s: Jesus says he came into the world for judgment so that those who don't see may see and those who see may become blind. When the Pharisees ask if they are also blind, he answers that if they were blind they would have no sin, but because they say they see, their sin remains. The physically blind man gains sight and also comes to belief, while the Pharisees who claim to see are rebuked.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: In John chapter 10, Jesus gives a parable of the sheep fold and then explains it, calling himself the door of the sheep and the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep and will bring other sheep into one flock. The Jews are divided over his words, some saying he has a demon and others pointing to his healing of the blind. At the Feast of the Dedication in Solomon's porch, the Jews demand he say plainly whether he is the Christ, and Jesus points to his works, says his sheep hear him, and declares 'I and the Father are one.' The Jews take up stones for what they call blasphemy, Jesus answers from Scripture and his works, and they try to seize him but he escapes beyond the Jordan, where many believe in him.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: Jesus tells the sheep fold parable, then identifies himself as the door and the good shepherd who lays down his life and takes it again by the Father's commandment. At the Feast of the Dedication he says his sheep hear him, that he and the Father are one, and defends himself against the charge of blasphemy by appealing to Scripture and his works. He escapes seizure and goes beyond the Jordan, where many believe in him.

l: God the Father, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: The Father is said to know Jesus as Jesus knows him, to love Jesus because he lays down his life, and to have given Jesus the commandment to lay down and take up his life. He is greater than all, and no one can snatch Jesus' sheep from his hand. Jesus declares 'I and the Father are one' and says the Father sanctified and sent him into the world.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: The Jews are divided over Jesus' words, some saying he has a demon and is insane, others citing the opening of the blind's eyes. They press him to say plainly if he is the Christ, then take up stones to stone him for blasphemy because, as they say, he being a man makes himself God. They seek to seize him again but he goes out of their hand.

l: sheep (Jesus' sheep), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: The sheep listen to the shepherd's voice, are called by name, and follow him but flee strangers. Jesus says his sheep hear his voice and follow him, are given eternal life, will never perish, and cannot be snatched from his or the Father's hand. He has other sheep not of this fold who will become one flock with one shepherd, and he tells the Jews they do not believe because they are not of his sheep.

l: shepherd (in the parable), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: In the parable the shepherd enters by the door, is opened to by the gatekeeper, calls his own sheep by name, leads them out and goes before them. Jesus contrasts him with the thief and robber who climb in another way. Jesus later identifies himself as the good shepherd, distinct from the hired hand who flees from the wolf.

l: the good shepherd parable, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: Jesus speaks the sheep fold parable in verses 1-5, and those listening do not understand it. He then explains it in two images: he is the door through which one is saved and finds pasture, and he is the good shepherd who knows his own and lays down his life, unlike the thief or the hired hand. The thief comes to steal, kill and destroy, while Jesus came that the sheep may have life abundantly.

l: Jesus' death and resurrection, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: Jesus says repeatedly that he lays down his life for the sheep. He states that the Father loves him because he lays down his life that he may take it again, that no one takes it from him, and that he has power to lay it down and take it up by the Father's commandment.

l: works of Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: Jesus says the works he does in his Father's name testify about him, and he asks the Jews for which of his many good works from the Father they stone him. He urges them to believe the works if they will not believe him, so they may know the Father is in him and he in the Father. Others cite the opening of the eyes of the blind as evidence against the charge of demon possession.

l: blasphemy, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 10
s: The Jews say they stone Jesus not for a good work but for blasphemy, because he, being a man, makes himself God. Jesus answers that the law calls those to whom God's word came 'gods' and asks why they say he blasphemes for saying he is the Son of God, whom the Father sanctified and sent.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Martha and Mary, falls sick, and Jesus delays two days before going to Judea despite his disciples' fear of the Jews. Jesus tells them Lazarus is dead, and Thomas urges the others to go and die with him. Martha and Mary each tell Jesus that Lazarus would not have died had he been there; Jesus tells Martha he is the resurrection and the life, weeps, and then calls Lazarus out of the tomb, who comes out bound in wrappings. Many of the Jews believe, but some report to the Pharisees, and the chief priests and Pharisees gather a council. Caiaphas says one man should die for the people, and they resolve to kill Jesus, who withdraws to Ephraim as the Passover nears and a command goes out to report where he is.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Jesus delays two days after hearing that Lazarus is sick, then goes to Judea and tells his disciples plainly that Lazarus is dead. He declares himself the resurrection and the life, weeps at the tomb, prays to the Father, and calls Lazarus out. Because the council resolves to kill him, he withdraws to Ephraim with his disciples, and the authorities order that anyone who knows where he is must report it.

l: Lazarus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Lazarus of Bethany, whom Jesus loves, falls sick and dies, and has been in the tomb four days when Jesus arrives. At Jesus' loud call he comes out bound hand and foot in wrappings with his face wrapped in a cloth, and Jesus says to free him and let him go.

l: Martha, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Martha, sister of Lazarus, sends word to Jesus about his sickness and goes out to meet him when he comes, telling him Lazarus would not have died had he been there. She confesses that he is the Christ, God's Son, who comes into the world, then secretly calls Mary. At the tomb she objects that there will be a stench after four days, and Jesus reminds her that belief means seeing God's glory.

l: Mary, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus, is identified as the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair. She stays in the house until Martha calls her, then falls at Jesus' feet and says Lazarus would not have died had he been there. Her weeping, and that of the Jews with her, leaves Jesus groaning in spirit and troubled.

l: Caiaphas, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Caiaphas, high priest that year, tells the council they know nothing and that it is advantageous for one man to die for the people so the whole nation does not perish. The text says he spoke as high priest, not of himself, prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation and also gather into one the scattered children of God.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Some of the Jews had recently tried to stone Jesus, and many come to console Martha and Mary. They weep, comment on Jesus' affection for Lazarus, and some ask why he who opened a blind man's eyes did not keep Lazarus from dying. Many who see the raising believe in him, but some go to the Pharisees and report what he did.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: The Pharisees receive a report from some of the Jews about what Jesus did. With the chief priests they gather a council, fear that everyone will believe in him, and take counsel to put him to death. They also command that anyone who knows where he is must report it so they can seize him.

l: the chief priests, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: The chief priests join the Pharisees in gathering a council, saying Jesus does many signs and fearing the Romans will take away their place and nation. They plan from that day to kill him and command that anyone who knows where he is must report it.

l: God, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Jesus says Lazarus' sickness is for the glory of God and that God's Son may be glorified by it. Martha says God will give Jesus whatever he asks, and Jesus thanks the Father for always listening to him, so that the crowd may believe the Father sent him.

l: Bethany, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Bethany is the village of Mary and Martha and the home of Lazarus. It is near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away, and many of the Jews gather there to console the sisters.

l: tomb (Lazarus's tomb), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Lazarus's tomb is a cave with a stone lying against it, and he has lain there four days when Jesus arrives. At Jesus' command the stone is taken away, and Lazarus comes out at his call.

l: Jesus' raising of Lazarus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
s: Jesus has the stone taken away, prays aloud so the crowd may believe the Father sent him, and cries with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out!" The dead man comes out, and many of the Jews who saw it believe in Jesus. The sign also prompts the council to plot his death.

l: resurrection, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 11
